                 NELDA HOWTON'S INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

Intervenor Nelda Howton, appearing pro se as an affected landowner, files this Initial Post-

Hearing Brief opposing approval of any route that uses Link F-20, including Route 894. This

brief relies on Mrs. Howton's sworn direct testimony and admitted exhibits, and on hearing

testimony that supports her position that Link F-20 would impose concentrated and avoidable

impacts on her residence, agricultural property, livestock operations, storm-damaged community,

safety, aesthetic values, and environmental integrity. (Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 1-2; Nelda

Howton Exs. 1-7.4.)


                                I. TABLE OF AUTHORITIES

Tex. Util. Code § 37.057
Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(a), (c)(4)
Tex. Util. Code § 37.156
16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101, including § 25.101(b)(3)(B)
16 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 22.71-.72
SOAH Order No. 6, PUC Interchange Item No. 788 (Apr. 20, 2026)

                                 II. STATEMENT OF CASE




                                              Page 2
 This proceeding concerns the Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and

LCRA Transmission Service Corporation (Applicants) to amend their Certificates of

Convenience and Necessity for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV

transmission line project. The statutory 180-day deadline is governed by Tex. Util. Code §

37.057. SOAH Order No. 6 adopted the procedural schedule, set April 27, 2026 as the

intervention deadline, May 13, 2026 as the deadline for intervenor testimony or statements of

position, June 8-12, 2026 as the hearing on the merits, and June 19, 2026 as the deadline for

initial briefs. (SOAH Order No. 6 at 4-8, PUC Interchange Item No. 788.)

Mrs. Howton filed sworn direct testimony as a pro se intervenor and affected landowner. Her

testimony explains that she resides at 12600 FM 2843, Salado, Texas, that her testimony is based

on personal observations and firsthand landowner knowledge, and that she opposes all routes

using Link F-20, including Route 894. (Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 1.)

The evidentiary record includes testimony from Applicants' routing witnesses and PUC Staff

witness John Poole concerning Link F-20, Route 894, Route 296, Route 899, Route 499,

habitable-structure counts, field verification, cultural-resource review, storm recovery, and

alternative routes. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 115:15-119:8, 120:18-124:8; Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 51:8-

58:20, 91:21-92:4, 205:11-207:10.)


                                   III. ISSUES PRESENTED

1. Whether the routing criteria in Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(c)(4) support rejection of routes that

use Link F-20 because those routes would impose concentrated impacts on Mrs. Howton's home,

property, livestock, agricultural operations, family use, storm recovery, safety, aesthetic values,

and environmental integrity.




                                               Page 3
 2. Whether Applicants adequately verified and evaluated localized facts affecting Link F-20,

including habitable structures, cultural resources, field conditions, storm-damaged conditions,

and site-specific environmental and archaeological concerns.

3. Whether the record supports selecting Staff witness John Poole's second-place Route 296,

Route 899, Route 499, Route 767, Route 295, or another route that avoids Link F-20 and better

minimizes impacts on residences, agriculture, community values, and environmental integrity.


                                IV. SUMMARY OF POSITION

The central issue for Mrs. Howton is not whether a transmission line may be needed somewhere.

The issue is whether Applicants' selected route fairly applies PURA and Commission routing

criteria to the people, property, and community resources that would bear the burden of a 765-kV

transmission line. Mrs. Howton's evidence shows that Link F-20 would be placed too close to her

residence and agricultural improvements and would impose avoidable harm on an established

rural community already affected by severe storm damage. (Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 1-2;

Nelda Howton Exs. 1, 3, 4.1-4.4.)

The record further supports her position because Applicants' witnesses confirmed that Link F-20

was added after the public meeting, that additional turning angles generally increase cost, that

there was no westward constraint requiring the 90-degree turn north, and that Applicants' routing

witness did not walk Link F-20 or speak with landowners along Link F-20 before proposing it.

(Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 120:18-124:8.)

The record also shows that site-specific weaknesses in the Link F-20 analysis matter. Applicants

acknowledged an additional potential habitable structure within 500 feet of Link F-20,

acknowledged that no site-specific Golden-cheeked Warbler habitat field survey was conducted



                                              Page 4
 on Link F-20 before route selection, acknowledged that the Environmental Assessment did not

reference the April 12, 2022 tornado in Cedar Valley, and acknowledged that no specific routing

criterion accounts for a corridor recovering from a declared natural disaster. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 4

at 51:8-55:23.)

For those reasons, Mrs. Howton requests that the ALJs recommend rejection of Route 894 and

any other route using Link F-20, and instead recommend Route 296, Route 899, Route 499,

Route 767, Route 295, or another non-F-20 route that better protects residences, agricultural

operations, community values, storm recovery, safety, historical and aesthetic values, and

environmental integrity. (Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 2; Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 57:4-58:20,

91:21-92:4, 205:11-207:10.)


                           V. APPLICABLE LEGAL STANDARD

Under PURA, the Commission may approve a certificate of convenience and necessity only after

considering the statutory factors relevant to public convenience and necessity and routing. Tex.

Util. Code § 37.056(a), (c)(4). For transmission-line routing, the Commission must consider,

among other factors, community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic

values, environmental integrity, and the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to

consumers. Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(c)(4).

Commission routing rules also require consideration of prudent avoidance. 16 Tex. Admin. Code

§ 25.101(b)(3)(B). In the hearing record, Applicants explained that habitable-structure counts are

used as an indicator for route comparisons and how well a route performs as far as routing near

structures. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 82:17-83:25.)




                                              Page 5
 For a pro se landowner, the statutory factors should be applied to the actual facts in the record,

including direct testimony and exhibits from landowners who know the local property,

community, land uses, storm damage, vegetation, livestock operations, and safety conditions.

Mrs. Howton's direct testimony provides those facts for her home and agricultural property.

(Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 1-2; Nelda Howton Exs. 1-7.4.)


                                        VI. ARGUMENT


A. Link F-20 would impose concentrated residential and property-use impacts on Mrs.

Howton.

Mrs. Howton testified that the proposed 765-kV line would be located approximately 242 feet

from the centerline to her residence and approximately 143 feet from the nearest transmission

structures and conductor locations, as reflected in her aerial proximity exhibit. (Nelda Howton

Direct Test. at 1; Nelda Howton Ex. 3.) Those distances show a direct, close, and personal

impact on the residence and daily use of the property.

The property is not vacant or unused land. Mrs. Howton testified that her family owns

approximately 47 acres used for cattle production, horse activities, deer hunting, poultry

production, gardening, and general agricultural operations, with barns, fencing, corrals, a

residence, livestock uses, and family outdoor activities. (Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 1; Nelda

Howton Exs. 1, 5.1-5.3.)

The close proximity of Link F-20 to Mrs. Howton's home, combined with active agricultural and

family use, makes Link F-20 a concentrated burden on one rural homestead and its surrounding

uses. These facts should receive substantial weight under community values, aesthetic values,




                                               Page 6
 environmental integrity, and prudent avoidance. Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(c)(4); 16 Tex. Admin.

Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B).


B. Link F-20 does not adequately protect community values.

Community values include more than population counts or map labels. In this case, community

values include the rural residential character of the Cedar Valley/Salado area, agricultural life,

family use of land, community recovery after the April 2022 tornado, and the role of First Cedar

Valley Baptist Church as a local cultural and historical community resource. (Nelda Howton

Direct Test. at 1-2; Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 115:15-119:8; Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 54:24-55:3.)

The hearing record supports Mrs. Howton's community-values concern. Applicants' routing

witness did not dispute that First Cedar Valley Baptist Church has local or regional significance,

did not dispute its age, and agreed that if it is a church of cultural significance to the community,

he did not dispute that significance. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 117:8-118:25.) The record also

reflects that the church is approximately 720 feet from the centerline. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at

119:3-8.)

Applicants' process for cultural-resource review relied on recorded database sources and did not

capture every local cultural value. The routing witness explained that the table was based on

specific sources, not every community-significant resource. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 117:8-119:8.)

That matters because PURA requires the Commission to consider community values and

historical and aesthetic values, not merely database entries. Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(c)(4).


C. Tornado recovery evidence supports avoiding additional infrastructure burdens in this

area.




                                               Page 7
 Mrs. Howton's sworn testimony explains that the community recently experienced significant

tornado damage and remains in recovery. Her exhibits include the Governor's Disaster

Proclamation and photographs of tornado damage, fallen trees, damaged fencing, debris, and

damage affecting property use and access. (Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 2; Nelda Howton Exs.

4.1-4.4.)

Applicants' witness confirmed that the Environmental Assessment and Routing Study contains

no reference to the April 12, 2022 EF3 tornado that tracked through Cedar Valley along FM

2843. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 54:10-14.) The same witness acknowledged reading testimony from

the area that approximately 70 homes and 3 church buildings were damaged and confirmed that

First Cedar Valley Baptist Church, rebuilt after the tornado, sits about 700 feet from the

proposed F-20 centerline. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 54:15-55:3.)

Applicants further confirmed that their routing criteria do not contain a specific criterion

accounting for a corridor that experienced a federally or state-declared natural disaster, and do

not specifically account for post-disaster recovery. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 55:4-23.) These

admissions support Mrs. Howton's request that the ALJs give greater weight to her local storm-

recovery evidence and avoid adding a major 765-kV transmission line burden to a recovering

rural community.


D. Link F-20 would adversely affect agricultural, livestock, and family recreational uses.

Mrs. Howton's property supports cattle production, equine activities, poultry production,

gardening, hunting, and family outdoor use. These uses are not incidental; they define the

function and character of the property. (Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 1; Nelda Howton Exs. 5.1-

5.3.)




                                               Page 8
 Transmission-line routing should account for practical impacts on fencing, access, livestock

behavior, livestock safety, family outdoor use, property maintenance, and the continued

agricultural use of the property. Mrs. Howton's photographs of a filly delivered on the property,

cattle grazing operations, and poultry operations demonstrate active rural uses that would be

directly affected by routing and construction. (Nelda Howton Exs. 5.1-5.3.)

Those land uses are relevant under PURA's community-values, aesthetic-values, and

environmental-integrity factors because they show that Link F-20 would burden an active rural

homestead rather than merely crossing unused open land. Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(c)(4).


E. Wildfire, vegetation, and emergency-response concerns support rejecting Link F-20.

Mrs. Howton testified that the area contains heavy vegetation, dry grass, cedar debris, and other

conditions that increase wildfire risk. Her exhibits include a firefighter wildfire safety statement

and photographs of dried cedar, cedar and blue stem grass, and King Ranch blue stem grass.

(Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 2; Nelda Howton Exs. 7.1-7.4.)

The firefighter wildfire safety statement describes Cedar Valley's major 2022 tornado damage,

remaining brush piles and tree debris, and the risk of adding a 765-kV high-voltage transmission

line through a high-risk wildfire zone. (Nelda Howton Ex. 7.1.) The vegetation photographs

further show dried cedar, dense cedar and grass conditions, and King Ranch blue stem grass

conditions that support routing concerns involving vegetation management, fire risk, and

emergency response. (Nelda Howton Exs. 7.2-7.4.)

A 765-kV transmission line should not be routed in a manner that unnecessarily increases

wildfire, vegetation-management, and emergency-access concerns for a rural property and

community. The ALJs should give substantial weight to this evidence under environmental



                                               Page 9
 integrity, community values, and safety-related routing considerations. Tex. Util. Code §

37.056(c)(4).


F. Health, noise, visual, and quality-of-life concerns support giving greater weight to local

landowner evidence.

Mrs. Howton is not offering expert medical testimony. Her direct testimony states that, to the

extent she discusses publicly available studies, scientific materials, governmental publications, or

articles, she does so only to explain the basis of her concerns and understanding as a layperson.

(Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 1; Nelda Howton Ex. 6.)

Her concerns about visual impacts, audible corona noise, reduced enjoyment and use of property,

potential effects on livestock behavior and agricultural operations, fire risk, and long-term

impacts to property value and future residential use are proper landowner concerns for route

selection. (Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 1-2; Nelda Howton Exs. 1, 3, 6, 7.1-7.4.)

The record also supports a cautious approach because Applicants acknowledged that this would

be the first 765-kV line built in Texas and that there is no real-life Texas experience with such a

line. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 84:3-85:4.) Applicants further confirmed that all 122 filed routes are

acceptable and that the Commission may consider route-specific factors, including prudent

avoidance and the type of habitable structures a route is near. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 108:13-22.)


G. Staff-supported Route 296 and non-F-20 alternatives should be preferred.

Mrs. Howton's direct testimony supported Route 767 or another route that minimizes impacts to

residences, agricultural operations, and established rural communities. (Nelda Howton Direct

Test. at 1-2.) The hearing record also supports her post-hearing request for Preferred Route 296,

Route 899, Route 499, Route 767, Route 295, or another non-F-20 route.


                                              Page 10
 PUC Staff witness John Poole confirmed that Route 296 was his second-place route, very close

behind Route 487, and that he ranked Route 296 above Applicants' Route 894. (Hearing Tr. Vol.

4 at 91:21-92:4.) This directly supports Mrs. Howton's request that the ALJs recommend Route

296 rather than Route 894 or any route using Link F-20.

The record also supports non-F-20 alternatives that substitute Link F-21 for Link F-20.

Applicants acknowledged that Route 899 avoids Links F-20 and F-23, is shorter than Route 894,

and is very close in cost to Route 894. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 57:4-58:12.) When the questioning

focused on habitable structures and cost, Applicants did not identify a material basis to prefer

Route 894 over Route 899 on those two factors. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 58:13-21.)

PUC Staff witness Poole also confirmed that Route 499 keeps Route 487's western alignment

while replacing F-20 and F-23 with Segments F-21, E-9, and G-71; that Route 487 and Route

499 both have 96 habitable structures within 500 feet of the centerline; that they have the same

length across endangered-species habitat; that the cost difference is about $2 million, or one-

tenth of one percent; and that Route 499 removes the line from the F-20 and F-23 corridor.

(Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 205:11-207:10.)

These route comparisons show that rejecting Link F-20 would not require the Commission to

abandon the project. The record identifies feasible non-F-20 routes that better protect Mrs.

Howton's residence, agricultural operations, livestock uses, community values, tornado recovery,

wildfire safety, aesthetic values, and environmental integrity. (Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 1-2;

Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 57:4-58:20, 91:21-92:4, 205:11-207:10.)


    VII. PROPOSED FINDINGS SUPPORTED BY MRS. HOWTON'S TESTIMONY




                                              Page 11
 1. Nelda Howton is an affected landowner and pro se intervenor in this docket. (Nelda Howton

Direct Test. at 1.)

2. Mrs. Howton's testimony is based on personal observations, firsthand knowledge, and

experience as a landowner whose residence, agricultural operations, livestock, water resources,

and quality of life would be directly impacted by the proposed 765-kV transmission line. (Nelda

Howton Direct Test. at 1.)

3. Mrs. Howton opposes all proposed routes utilizing Link F-20, including Route 894. (Nelda

Howton Direct Test. at 1-2.)

4. Mrs. Howton requests approval of Route 296, Route 899, Route 499, Route 767, Route 295, or

another route that avoids Link F-20 and better minimizes impacts to residences, agricultural

operations, and established rural communities. (Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 2; Hearing Tr. Vol.

4 at 57:4-58:20, 91:21-92:4, 205:11-207:10.)

5. Mrs. Howton's property is used for cattle production, horse activities, deer hunting, poultry

production, gardening, and general agricultural operations. (Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 1;

Nelda Howton Exs. 5.1-5.3.)

6. Mrs. Howton presented evidence of proximity impacts, including the closeness of the

proposed 765-kV line to her residence and improvements. (Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 1;

Nelda Howton Ex. 3.)

7. Mrs. Howton presented evidence concerning storm damage, tornado recovery, wildfire risk,

vegetation conditions, livestock operations, and family use of the property. (Nelda Howton

Direct Test. at 1-2; Nelda Howton Exs. 4.1-4.4, 5.1-5.3, 7.1-7.4.)




                                               Page 12
 8. Applicants' Environmental Assessment did not reference the April 12, 2022 EF3 tornado

through Cedar Valley, and Applicants had no specific routing criterion accounting for a declared-

disaster corridor or post-disaster recovery. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 54:10-55:23.)

9. Applicants did not walk Link F-20 or speak with landowners along Link F-20 before

proposing it. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 123:23-124:8.)

10. The routing factors in PURA § 37.056(c)(4) support giving weight to Mrs. Howton's

evidence concerning community values, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity,

and direct property impacts. Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(c)(4).

11. Routes utilizing Link F-20 would impose concentrated and avoidable impacts on Mrs.

Howton and the surrounding rural community. (Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 1-2; Nelda

Howton Exs. 1-7.4.)

12. Route 296, Route 899, Route 499, Route 767, Route 295, or another non-F-20 route would

better satisfy PURA § 37.056(c)(4) than Route 894 if Route 894 uses Link F-20. (Hearing Tr.

Vol. 4 at 57:4-58:20, 91:21-92:4, 205:11-207:10.)


                             VIII. CONCLUSION AND PRAYER

For the reasons stated above, Intervenor Nelda Howton respectfully requests that the

Administrative Law Judges recommend that the Commission reject Route 894 and any other

route utilizing Link F-20. Mrs. Howton further requests that the Administrative Law Judges

recommend Route 296, Route 899, Route 499, Route 767, Route 295, or another route that

avoids Link F-20 and better protects residences, agricultural operations, community values,

storm recovery, wildfire safety, aesthetic values, and environmental integrity. (Nelda Howton




                                              Page 13
 Direct Test. at 1-2; Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 57:4-58:20, 91:21-92:4, 205:11-207:10; Tex. Util. Code

§ 37.056(c)(4).)

Mrs. Howton requests all other relief to which she may be justly entitled.

Respectfully submitted,

                           V. APPLICABLE LEGAL STANDARD


Under PURA, the Commission may approve a certificate of convenience and necessity only after

considering the statutory factors relevant to public convenience and necessity and routing. Tex.

Util. Code § 37.056(a), (c)(4). For transmission-line routing, the Commission must consider,

among other factors, community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic

values, environmental integrity, and the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to

consumers. Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(c)(4).


Commission routing rules also require consideration of prudent avoidance. 16 Tex. Admin. Code

§ 25.101(b)(3)(B). In the hearing record, Applicants explained that habitable-structure counts are

used as an indicator for route comparisons and how well a route performs as far as routing near

structures. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 82:17-83:25.)




                                              Page 5
 For a pro se landowner, the statutory factors should be applied to the actual facts in the record,

including direct testimony and exhibits from landowners who know the local property,

community, land uses, storm damage, vegetation, livestock operations, and safety conditions.

Mrs. Howton's direct testimony provides those facts for her home and agricultural property.

(Nelda Howton Direct Test. at 1-2; Nelda Howton Exs. 1-7.4.)
